horse E55: Depicted Type P199 represents instance of type is used, rather than P138 represents, because its scope note covers exactly the case where "the identity of the thing depicted is unknown or unrecorded, but is clearly a particular thing of that type". The same scope note says that a visual item depicting the concept rather than an instance should instead take P138 represents : E55 Type. If the readings recorded below are right and the figure is emblematic - a tribal symbol, or a solar horse - then P138 represents : E55 Type "horse" would be the correct property. The article does not settle this, and neither does this model. Contested reading E55: Note Type
It has long been debated whether the figure was intended to represent a horse or some other animal, such as a dog or a sabre-toothed cat. The article attributes neither the dog reading nor the sabre-toothed cat reading to any named person, so neither is modelled as an assertion by anyone. It has been called a horse since the 11th century at least. Contested reading E55: Note Type
The horse is thought to represent a tribal symbol, perhaps connected with the builders of Uffington Castle. The article gives no author for this reading. Contested reading E55: Note Type
Some scholars have compared the figure to the Celtic goddess Epona, or the later Rhiannon of the Mabinogi. The article names none of them. Contested reading E55: Note Type

Francis Wise wrote in 1736 that "the ceremony of scouring the Horse, from time immemorial, has been solemnized by a numerous concourse of people from all the villages roundabout", which is why the outer bound is left open at its start. The inner bound runs from the first festival known, in 1755, to the present. Statement E55: Note Type

The maintenance is what has kept the figure in existence: if regular cleaning is halted, the figure quickly becomes obscured. Description E55: Note Type

until the late 19th century E52: Time-Span time immemorial - 1899 E61: Time Primitive
Until the late 19th century the horse was scoured every seven years as part of a more general local fair held on the hill; after the work was done a rural festival was held, sponsored by the lord of the manor. The first such festival known took place in 1755 and they lasted until 1857, when 30,000 people turned up and were "too rowdy". The fair and its sports are reception rather than restoration and are recorded here only as the occasion of the work. The article does not say that the lord of the manor owned the figure, and no ownership is inferred from the sponsorship. Description E55: Note Type
